segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was I am from estar? I am?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estoy. If you want to say I'm there for you, I'm there for you, you know, in this supportive way, you don't have to say there to begin with because we are using estar and not ser, it kind of makes that there a little redundant. We feel that already in estar that's referring to states, locations, and states. So we don't need to say there, we can just say I'm for you. I'm for you using estar. What for do you think you need?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Para.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say I'm there for you talking to a friend?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy para ti.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estoy para ti. Good. To say I'm here because of you, then we are not going to use para. We don't even really need to say here.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: If it's still estoy, it still implies location.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It kind of just gives you the feeling. Actually when you knock on somebody's door and you are calling for them, you will just say ¿estás?, you don't say are you there. Or if you're on internet, ¿estás? you will write in the messenger. If you call somebody up and you want to speak to Juan, you will not say is Juan there, you will just say ¿está Juan?, Juan ¿está?. So I am here because of you, formal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy por usted.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estoy por usted. For you, informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy por ti.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estoy por ti. So this would be because of you. How would you say I have come because of you? I have come because of you. Informal, I have come because of you.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, the first bit is he. He venido por ti.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He venido por ti. So whenever we want because of, we want to avoid the temptation to translate porque de, ah, because of. Good. So I have come because of you: he venido por ti. You could also say it is because of you that we have come, for example. It is because of you that we have come. And of course we can make the sentence perfectly if we think it through piece by piece. So it is because of you...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es por ti...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...that we have come.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...que hemos venido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es por ti que hemos venido. It is because of you that we have come. Good. Another use of por, so we are seeing that por is much more flexible than para, another use of por is if you want to say for in the sense of exchanging this one for that one, to exchange something for something else, then also we use por. Cambiar, cambiar means to change.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you want to say I would change this one for that one, I would change this one for that one, and with this one and that one let's refer to a masculine thing. So I would change is the first step.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cambiaría...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Aha. This one, a masculine thing?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Este...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. For that one, masculine thing?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Por ese.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Take away the T. Good. Cambiaría este por ese. I would change this one for that one.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say I would change these ones for those ones, masculine or mixed objects? I would change these ones for those ones.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cambiaría estos por esos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Cambiaría estos por esos. Very good. What if they were feminine things?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cambiaría estas por esas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Cambiaría estas por esas. Good. Would you change these ones for those ones, speaking informally? Would you change these ones for those ones? Still feminine things.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Cambiarías estas por esas?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Cambiarías estas por esas? Wouldn't you change these ones for those ones? Still feminine?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿No cambiarías estas por esas?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Go on.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Por qué no cambiaría...? ¿Por qué no cambiaría estas por esas?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Still think it through though, huh?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sorry, ¿por qué no cambiarías estas por esas?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. We don't want to stop thinking. You'll be able to relax that, ah, as you go on, but at the beginning you want to be very insistent on your thinking so you install correct structural habits or grammatical habits. We don't really use much grammatical terminology, but everything we're seeing here is grammar, of course, it's all structure.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ah, something I should mention is that if you're chatting online, if you're practicing your Spanish online, you might see por written as an x, as a shortcut, because por is also what you use in like times tables. Ocho por ocho is 8 x 8. So you might see gracias por venir as gracias x venir. And if you have the habit of writing kisses with an x, this can be very confusing to Spanish speakers.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So gracias por venir reminds us, this nice hook that we will hear a lot, gracias por venir, reminds us that we have two words for for: para, something being for you, quite literally, and then por, which is much more flexible in meaning.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The other thing that we learn from the sentence gracias por venir is that after prepositions, so these little group of words, we've seen para, por, de, en, con, a, we've seen quite a few of them, following these words in English we put -ing: thank you for coming. But in Spanish we just put the to form: gracias por venir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say thank you for calling? Thank you for calling. If you forget call, you could think of, uh, what's your name or how are you called, because it's something that people tend to have heard somewhere.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Gracias por llamar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Gracias por llamar. And if you wanted to say thanks for calling me, you could say that as well?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Gracias por llamarme.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Gracias por llamarme. So after prepositions we don't use the -ing, we want to resist any temptation to put the -ing form after the preposition. This is negative language transfer, things that are not the same between English and Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was I am from estar?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estoy. And you remember how to say tired in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cansado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Cansado. So how do you say I am tired?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy cansado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But you being a female?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cansada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estoy cansada. So, if you want to say I'm tired of dancing, cooking, cleaning, it's all going to be with the to form. What was to work?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Trabajar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Trabajar. How would you say I am tired of working?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy cansada de trabajar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Estoy cansada de trabajar. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For one of the pasts that we saw, for the line in the past, so when we're referring to like a period of time in the past, for -ar verbs we had the -aba base ending. So how would you say I was from estar?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estaba. I was tired of working?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estaba cansada de trabajar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estaba cansada de trabajar. Good. I was tired of working. Good. We were tired of working, and let's be a masculine or a mixed group. We were tired of working.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estábamos cansados de trabajar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Estábamos cansados de trabajar. Good. If you want to say, uh, something like it's a way of doing it, it's a way of doing it, the word for way is form, form, a form of doing it. And how do you think form might be in Spanish if you had to guess it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Forma.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Forma. Good. So how would you say a way of doing it? What was to do, or to make?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hacer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It is a way of doing it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es una forma de hacerlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es una forma de hacerlo. Good. I don't believe in arguing like this, in this way. I don't believe in arguing in this way. So...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To believe is creer, creer, and it has two E's, c-r-e-e-r, creer.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Creer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how do you say I don't believe?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No creo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No creo. What was creation?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Creación.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And what was to create?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Crear.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And what was I create?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Creo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. So we get this situation occasionally in Spanish that the I form of two different verbs will look the same. Creo, of course, could be from creer, to believe, or from crear, to create. So I don't believe...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No creo...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...in arguing. So to argue in Spanish you can use to discuss. This is the most common verb actually that's used for argue. Discuss is discutir, discutir.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So what do they use for discuss?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablar mostly, but you can use discutir as well for discuss, but it has a heavy connotation mostly, no? I mean if you argue with your boyfriend or your girlfriend, you use discutir, you say this. Argüir, argüir, which is argue, means to argue a point rather than to get in an argument. Discutir is more like to get in an argument. So it's, it's what we can call a false friend, words that look like they are the same, but they have a difference in meaning, and there are a few of them. We need to watch out for them between English and Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Another example would be actual, which doesn't mean actual, it means current. No? Mi trabajo actual, my current job. Actualmente means currently, at the moment, rather than actually. Mostly the vocabulary, the Latin English that we turn into Spanish is very reliable, but there are a few words that we want to watch out for.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Discutir is one of them. This doesn't really mean to discuss as much as it does to argue. So I don't believe in arguing...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No creo en discutir...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. In this way, we will say of this way rather than in this way.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: De esta forma.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So all together, I don't believe in arguing, in discussing, in this way?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No creo en discutir de esta forma.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No creo en discutir de esta forma. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So with this sentence gracias por venir, we are reminded how we have two words for for: por and para, and we need to have a think and decide which one we think is most appropriate before we translate for. And that after prepositions, we don't need to worry about making the -ing form of the verb, we just use the to form.
